title: Open-Set Semi-Supervised Text Classification with Latent Outlier Softening

problem.claim: Open-set semi-supervised text classification faces false positive inference caused by inadvertently including out-of-distribution texts during training.

gap.claim: Existing semi-supervised text classification research unrealistically assumes that unlabeled data contains only in-distribution texts.

contributions.claim: The paper develops baseline models using outlier detectors for hard out-of-distribution data filtering in a pipeline procedure.
The paper proposes a Latent Outlier Softening framework that integrates semi-supervised training and outlier detection within probabilistic latent variable modeling.
The framework softens out-of-distribution impacts using the Expectation-Maximization algorithm and weighted entropy maximization.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on three created datasets show that Latent Outlier Softening significantly outperforms the baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: Semi-supervised text classification reduces human annotation.
Assuming unlabeled data contains only in-distribution texts is unrealistic.
The paper considers open-set semi-supervised text classification, where unlabeled data contains out-of-distribution texts.
The main challenge is false positive inference from inadvertently including out-of-distribution texts during training.
The paper develops filtered baselines and proposes Latent Outlier Softening, reporting superior performance on three created datasets.

source_observation.claim: Unlabeled data may contain out-of-distribution texts that cause false positive inference during semi-supervised training.

interpretation.claim: Semi-supervised systems should account for latent contamination in unlabeled data rather than assume all unlabeled examples are in-distribution.

application.claim: Use outlier-aware filtering or probabilistic weighting when deploying semi-supervised text classification with potentially mixed unlabeled data.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the approach generalizes beyond the three created datasets.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify dataset sizes, domains, or construction procedures.
The abstract does not report quantitative performance values or statistical tests.
The abstract does not describe the baselines, model architecture, or implementation details.
